speaker: Doctor
text: Good morning, I am Dr. Agent. You have presented with a neck swelling; please describe exactly what you feel there, how long it has been present, and if you have noticed any pain, fever, or difficulty swallowing.

speaker: Patient
text: 50-year-old male. The patient reports a progressively increasing swelling on the nape of his neck for 2 months. He denies having a fever, pain, or any discharge from the swelling. He mentions a history of colon cancer for which he underwent colectomy at the age of 43. He also has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and osteoarthritis of the left knee. He takes insulin glargine, metformin, enalapril, and naproxen.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck to the left supraclavicular lymph node (Virchow's node), secondary to a primary head and neck malignancy, given the patient's history of colon cancer is unlikely to metastasize to this location without other systemic signs; however, the location (nape of neck/supraclavicular) and duration are highly suspicious for metastatic disease from an occult primary or spread from the known colon cancer via lymphatic or hematogenous routes, though the latter is less common for direct supraclavicular involvement without liver metastases. Given the history of colon cancer, we must rule out metastasis to the lymph nodes from the colon, but the location and lack of systemic symptoms like weight loss or fever suggest a primary head and neck cancer or metastasis from an occult primary. The most likely diagnosis is metastatic squamous cell carcinoma from an occult head and neck primary, given the location and duration
